In class eleven, Kamal had a Hindi essay due, and he did not write a line. Every evening he found a better task: sharpening pencils, rearranging shelves. Somewhere underneath he believed that if the essay came out weak, Vijay Sir would see that he was not as capable as everyone assumed. On the last night he scribbled a rushed page and handed in something much thinner than he could have written. Vijay Sir returned it with a single line of comment about effort.
At twenty, Kamal had a thesis chapter to begin and felt the same heavy dread. This time his friend Abhinav said, "Come to the library. Set a timer for twenty minutes. Write the ugliest paragraph you can." Kamal laughed, sat down and typed a messy opening that made no sense. The timer beeped. Abhinav peered at the page. "See? It's a start." Kamal hadn't planned to keep going, but he wrote another paragraph and then a third, and then the library lights blinked for closing.

qa.q: How long was the timer that Abhinav told Kamal to set?
qa.a: Abhinav told him to set a timer for twenty minutes.

qa.q: How does Kamal's way of starting at twenty differ from his approach to the Hindi essay?
qa.a: For the Hindi essay Kamal put it off every evening, afraid Vijay Sir would see he was not capable, and handed in something thin. At twenty he set a timer for twenty minutes in the library beside Abhinav and wrote the ugliest paragraph, and that messy start took away the dread so he kept writing.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he put off the Hindi essay?
qa.a: He was afraid and anxious about being judged, and busy tasks helped him avoid that uncomfortable feeling.

qa.q: What could Kamal try if the dread comes back before a big task?
qa.a: He can set a short timer, work near a friend or in a library, and allow himself a messy first paragraph before he polishes anything.

grounding: Avoidant delay to escape judgement (4056) later met by making the start easier with a timer, a library and a friend (3192); one person over years.

passage:
On Saturday, five-year-old Uday sat on the carpet ten minutes after breakfast and sighed. "I'm bored. Can I watch something?" Mummy Reena set out a basket of wooden spoons and a bowl of dry beans. "Show me what happens when these two meet." Uday frowned, then began pouring beans from bowl to bowl, and after a while he built a small bean mountain.
On Monday, at school, Uday sat in circle time while Urmila Ma'am read a story about a fox. His fingers tapped a quick beat against his knee. The child next to him leaned away. Urmila Ma'am glanced over and noticed his eyes were on the book, following each page turn. When the story paused she asked, "What might the fox do now?" Uday shot up his hand. "He'll hide in the barn!" His fingers were drumming again. Urmila Ma'am did not scold him. She had seen the same fingers at snack time, when he was bored, and they had looked different: slower, and his eyes had been wandering.

qa.q: What did Uday pour from bowl to bowl at home?
qa.a: He poured dry beans from bowl to bowl.

qa.q: What does Uday's behaviour on Saturday and Monday show about reading a child's restlessness?
qa.a: On Saturday the restless sigh came with real boredom, and time with simple things turned it into play. On Monday the tapping fingers went with close attention to the story, so Urmila Ma'am used the context and did not scold him, since the same movement can mean different things.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he said he was bored on Saturday?
qa.a: He felt restless and unsure what to do, which is why he asked for something to watch.

qa.q: What might Urmila Ma'am do if Uday's tapping bothers the child next to him?
qa.a: She could quietly give him a soft place to tap, or seat him where it is less distracting, without telling him off.

grounding: A child's boredom that becomes imagination with simple materials (4068) and finger-drumming that may mean focus rather than boredom (2204).

passage:
Ten minutes after lunch, Mehak wrapped both arms around Mummy Ganga's leg. "There's nothing to do." Mummy was folding clothes. "Can I have the tablet?" Mummy shook her head. "Not now." Mehak stayed clamped to her leg, dragging her feet as Mummy walked to the cupboard. She said the toys were boring, the books were boring, and everything was boring. She did not seem to know where to begin, and she did not know what she wanted instead.
The next afternoon it happened again. This time Papa Raghav put down his phone, sat on the floor and lined up five shoes in a row. "This is a train. Where should it go?" Mehak looked at the shoes. She dropped down and pushed the last one with a finger. "To the market," she said. Papa gave her a scarf for a tunnel, and then he stood up and went to make tea. When he returned, the train had gone through the tunnel twice, and Mehak was making the sound of a whistle.

qa.q: How many shoes did Papa Raghav line up to make a train?
qa.a: He lined up five shoes in a row.

qa.q: How do the two afternoons show Mehak's boredom and how it changed?
qa.a: On the first afternoon she clung to Mummy and said everything was boring, not knowing how to begin. On the second, Papa gave her a small start with shoes and a scarf, and she made up her own train game.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she clung to Mummy Ganga's leg and said there was nothing to do?
qa.a: She felt restless and a little lost, wanting company and something to do but not knowing how to start.

qa.q: What could Mummy Ganga try when Mehak next says she is bored?
qa.a: She can offer a few simple things and a first idea, then step away for a while so Mehak has time to make up her own game.

grounding: A child's first boredom shown as clinging and not knowing how to start (5208), and the same restless declaration (4068) eased when an adult gives a simple beginning.

Divyansh stood in the queue at orientation at nineteen and looked at the students' badges from famous schools. His own school was small and no one had heard of it. He told himself the selection had been a lucky slip. In the first seminar he stayed quiet, sure that the moment he spoke everyone would see through him. When Usha told him the seminar notes he shared were the clearest in the group, he said, "Anyone could have written those."
At twenty-two, Divyansh walked into his first office with a new lanyard and a nervous smile. The team was talking about "sprint velocity" and "the pipeline", and he pretended to nod. Bhavna, at the next desk, welcomed him warmly. "You'll pick it up." Divyansh smiled back, but at lunch he sat in front of his sandwich thinking that they must have picked the wrong resume. He was delighted to be hired, and terrified that they would find out.

qa.q: What did Divyansh say when Usha told him his seminar notes were the clearest?
qa.a: He said, "Anyone could have written those."

qa.q: How do Divyansh's thoughts at orientation and at his first office connect?
qa.a: In both places he compares himself with others and believes the selection was a mistake. The luck he blamed at nineteen returns as the fear at twenty-two that they picked the wrong resume.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling at lunch on his first day?
qa.a: He felt a mix of delight and fear. He was glad about the job but worried that everyone would discover he did not belong.

qa.q: How could Bhavna help Divyansh settle into the team?
qa.a: Bhavna could explain the unfamiliar terms in plain words and tell him it is normal to ask, so he does not have to pretend to understand.

grounding: Feeling like a fraud after admission to a top college (4092) recurs as arrival anxiety in a first job (3226); one person across years.

passage:
At five, Devika stood at the door of a neighbour's birthday party and tucked herself behind Mummy Hansa's legs. Balloons bobbed. A boy called her name, and she pressed her face into the folds of Mummy's kurta. Mummy did not push her forward. She rested a hand on Devika's shoulder and said, "We can stand here and watch." After a while Devika peeked out at the cake table. Later she moved to a chair at the edge, still holding a fistful of Mummy's dupatta.
At fifteen, Devika skipped a class presentation by saying she had a headache. Within weeks she stopped opening the class group chat and left her phone face-down when friends rang. She turned down the school picnic. Each no felt like a small relief, and each made the next yes harder. Papa Darshan noticed she barely left her room. He sat down beside her. "You used to love the picnic. Want to tell me what feels scary?" Devika stared at her hands. Later he called the school counsellor, and Devika agreed to talk to her.

qa.q: Where did Devika hide at the neighbour's birthday party?
qa.a: She tucked herself behind Mummy Hansa's legs at the door.

qa.q: How does Devika's avoidance at five compare with what happens at fifteen?
qa.a: At five Devika hid behind Mummy Hansa's legs, and gentle nearness at the door let her peek out and move to a chair. At fifteen, skipping one presentation grew into leaving the group chat, phone calls and the picnic, so each no made the next yes harder and Papa Darshan called the school counsellor.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she said she had a headache to skip the presentation?
qa.a: She was afraid and anxious, and getting out of it felt like relief, though her fear stayed hidden behind the excuse.

qa.q: What did Papa Darshan do well when he saw Devika staying in her room?
qa.a: He sat beside her and asked gently what felt scary instead of pushing, and then arranged for her to talk to the school counsellor.

grounding: A young child's hiding at a party, where nearness eases fear (3921), and the teenager's widening avoidance loop (3287): same girl over years.

passage:
At five, Nilesh clung to Mummy Nandini's leg outside the wedding hall and would not say hello to the aunties. "Say namaste, beta," someone urged. He tightened his grip. Mummy crouched down. "We'll stand by the pillar until you feel ready." Nilesh stayed there with his cheek against her side, and by the time the music started he was peeking around the pillar at the dancers.
At fifteen, Nilesh held a folded paper of practised sentences in his pocket. He had rehearsed the answer to a question about the poem for two hours, and when the teacher asked it, he lowered his eyes and said he did not know. He skipped the school trip and the science club party. His friend Zeenat noticed and asked, "Do you want to come and sit with us at the canteen?" Nilesh nodded but did not come. That evening Mummy sat with him and said gently, "This looks like a big worry, and I think someone who helps with this could make it lighter. Shall we talk to the school counsellor together?"

qa.q: How long had Nilesh practised his answer about the poem?
qa.a: He had rehearsed the answer for two hours.

qa.q: How is Nilesh's behaviour at the wedding hall like, and unlike, his behaviour in class at fifteen?
qa.a: At the wedding hall Nilesh clung to Mummy Nandini's leg and stood by the pillar until he was ready. At fifteen he rehearsed sentences for hours, lowered his eyes and skipped the school trip and the science club party, so the fear of embarrassment shrank his life and Mummy suggested the school counsellor.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he lowered his eyes and said he did not know the answer?
qa.a: He felt afraid of embarrassment, so even though he had practised the answer, he could not risk saying it.

qa.q: How could Zeenat keep supporting Nilesh?
qa.a: Zeenat could keep inviting him without pressure, sit with him where it is quiet, and let him join at his own pace.

grounding: A small child's clinging at a wedding (3921) and a teenager's intense fear of being judged that shrinks his life (4372), with gentle support in both.
